section.title: Aaron's Staff Becomes a Serpent
section.sectionRationale: A short, self-contained prologue to the plague cycle: God's final briefing to Moses about the hardening ahead, then the sign before Pharaoh's own court, where Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs, ending on the first note of hardened refusal.
section.thesis: Before a single plague falls, God stages a small preview of the whole contest: Egypt's magicians can copy the sign, but Aaron's staff swallows theirs, showing that every power Egypt can muster will be overmatched and ultimately consumed by the LORD.
section.frameNote: Two scenes: God's commission of Moses as like God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as prophet, and His warning that Pharaoh's heart will be hardened; the sign of the staff and serpent before Pharaoh, matched then swallowed.

units.label: Like God to Pharaoh
units.note: the commission repeated, the hardening foretold

verses.text: The LORD answered Moses, “See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet.
You are to speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go out of his land.
But I will {{chazaq2|harden}} Pharaoh's heart, and though I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,
Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay My hand on Egypt, and by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them.”
So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them.
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron,
“When Pharaoh tells you, ‘Perform a miracle,’ you are to say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh,’ and it will become a {{tannin|serpent}}.”
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw his staff down before Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a serpent.
But Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt, and they also did the same things by their magic arts.
Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent. But Aaron's staff swallowed up the other staffs.
Still, Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

chazaq2.gloss: To harden or make strong. God states plainly, before any plague, that He will harden Pharaoh's heart; this divine hardening runs alongside Pharaoh's own repeated self-hardening throughout the plague narrative, a tension Scripture never fully resolves but never denies.

tannin.gloss: A large serpent, sea monster, or dragon, a stronger word than the ordinary nachash used for Moses' staff-turned-snake in chapter 4. Before Pharaoh's own court, the sign is escalated, and Aaron's tannin swallows the magicians' own.

basic.context: God gives Moses and Aaron their final instructions before the confrontation with Pharaoh truly begins. God warns that He will harden Pharaoh's heart so that the coming plagues will be needed to force Israel's release. As a first sign, Aaron throws down his staff and it becomes a serpent, but Pharaoh's own magicians copy the trick, until Aaron's staff swallows all of theirs.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history that introduces one of the Bible's hardest and most honestly presented tensions: God says plainly that He will harden Pharaoh's heart, even before Pharaoh hardens his own heart later in the story. The passage does not shy away from this mystery; it states it directly and lets the tension stand.
basic.originalLanguages: God says He will chazaq, harden or strengthen, Pharaoh's heart, language that recurs eighteen times through the plague cycle, sometimes with God as the subject and sometimes with Pharaoh himself. Aaron's staff becomes a tannin, a larger and more fearsome serpent than the ordinary nachash of chapter 4, swallowing the magicians' identical signs.
basic.typology: The serpent that swallows serpents pictures a small preview of the whole exodus contest: every counterfeit power Egypt can produce is ultimately overmatched and consumed by the LORD's greater power, a pattern echoed whenever God's true power exposes and outlasts imitation and false religion.
basic.christ: Paul draws directly on the imagery of these magicians opposing Moses, naming them Jannes and Jambres, 2 Timothy 3:8, as a pattern of those who oppose the truth in the last days, whose folly, like Pharaoh's magicians, will eventually be plain to all, just as Christ's truth exposes and outlasts every counterfeit.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over the hardening of a human heart, a mystery Scripture states plainly here without explaining away Pharaoh's real responsibility for his own choices. He is also patient, giving Pharaoh sign after sign before the actual plagues of judgment begin.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Timothy 3:8-9 names the magicians and compares them to those who oppose the truth. Romans 9:17-18 draws directly on this hardening language to discuss God's sovereign purposes. Revelation 12:9 uses similar serpent and dragon imagery for the ancient enemy of God's people.
basic.oneStory: This is the opening bell of the plague contest: a small sign before the great ones, showing that Egypt's best counterfeits will be swallowed by the LORD's power. It sets the terms for everything that follows and anticipates how every false power opposed to God is ultimately overmatched by Him.

context.literary:
These thirteen verses are the overture to the plague narrative. They sit between the call of Moses, which closed with his second complaint about his 'uncircumcised lips,' Exodus 6:30, and the first plague at the Nile, Exodus 7:14. God's answer to the complaint opens the chapter: 'See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh,' verse 1. The man who could not speak is given a spokesman, and the roles are set out as a small picture of prophecy itself, God speaking to Moses, Moses to Aaron, Aaron to Pharaoh.

The scene has two panels, a word from God, verses 1 to 7, and a sign before Pharaoh, verses 8 to 13, and each records the same obedience: 'Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded,' verses 6 and 10. The first panel also works as a table of contents for chapters 7 to 14. It names the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, the multiplied signs and wonders, Pharaoh's refusal to listen, the mighty acts of judgment, the going out of Israel's divisions, and the goal, 'the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD,' verse 5. Each of those threads will be pulled in turn.

The second panel introduces the pattern the first plagues will follow. God gives an instruction, the sign is performed, the magicians match it, and Pharaoh's heart is hardened 'just as the LORD had said,' verse 13. That closing formula returns at Exodus 7:22, 8:15, 8:19 and 9:12, so this opening scene teaches the reader how to read the ones that follow.

Within the pattern there is a twist that the later plagues will widen. The magicians can imitate, but they cannot undo or overcome. Aaron's staff swallows theirs, verse 12. By the third plague they fail altogether, Exodus 8:18-19, and by the sixth they cannot even stand before Moses, Exodus 9:11. The rivalry is lost from the first move.
context.historical:
The scene is set in a royal audience, and the first hearers would have pictured the Egyptian court well. Pharaoh summons three groups in verse 11: 'wise men,' 'sorcerers,' and 'magicians.' The last word, chartummim, is generally thought to be borrowed from an Egyptian title for a class of lector priests, learned men who handled sacred texts and ritual. The same word describes the experts who failed Pharaoh in Joseph's day, Genesis 41:8, and it reappears in Babylon, Daniel 1:20 and 2:2. In each case the court's wisdom meets the God of Israel and falls short.

Serpents carried heavy meaning in Egypt. The rearing cobra, the uraeus, was worn on the front of Pharaoh's crown as a sign of royal and divine protection. A staff turned into a serpent before the throne was not a party trick; it spoke the language of royal power. When Aaron's serpent swallows the court's serpents, the symbolism is pointed. Egyptian literature also told of lector priests working wonders, such as making a wax crocodile come to life, so a contest of this kind would have been easy for Israel to picture.

How the magicians did 'the same things,' verse 11, is not explained. Snake handlers in the region have long been able to make a cobra rigid, and some suggest that was the method; others think of real occult power. The text simply calls it 'their magic arts' and moves quickly to the outcome.

Verse 7 gives Moses' age as eighty and Aaron's as eighty-three. Stephen's speech divides Moses' life into forties: forty when he went out to his brothers, Acts 7:23, eighty at the bush, Acts 7:30, and a hundred and twenty at his death, Deuteronomy 34:7. These were not young men seeking a career but old men sent against the most powerful ruler of their world.
context.canonical:
The staff that becomes a serpent here recalls the first sign given to Moses at the bush, Exodus 4:2-5, which was meant to persuade Israel. Now a similar sign is performed before Pharaoh. The contrast in the Hebrew words, noted in the BSB footnote, is part of the point: the snake of Exodus 4:3 was a nachash, while this one is a tannin, a word Scripture uses for the great creatures of the sea and for the dragon God defeats.

That second use sets the passage in a wide canonical frame. God created 'the great sea creatures,' Genesis 1:21. The psalmist remembers the exodus as the time when God 'divided the sea' and 'smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea,' Psalm 74:13. Isaiah calls on the arm of the LORD that 'pierced through the dragon,' Isaiah 51:9, and looks ahead to the day when He will 'slay the dragon of the sea,' Isaiah 27:1. Ezekiel addresses Pharaoh himself as the 'great monster who lies among his rivers,' Ezekiel 29:3. Revelation gathers the imagery into 'the great dragon... that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan,' Revelation 12:9.

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart becomes a warning for later generations. The Philistine priests ask, 'Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?' 1 Samuel 6:6. Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh from Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9:17 and concludes that God 'hardens whom He wants to harden,' Romans 9:18. Hebrews 3:13 urges believers to exhort one another daily so that none of them 'may be hardened by sin's deceitfulness.'

The magicians themselves reappear by name in 2 Timothy 3:8-9, where Paul calls them Jannes and Jambres, names preserved in Jewish tradition rather than in Exodus. They become the pattern of all who resist the truth with imitation power, and whose folly is eventually exposed.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wants Israel to understand the contest before it begins. Everything that follows, the refusals, the relenting and hardening, the escalating plagues, is announced here in advance, so that no one reading chapters 7 to 14 will conclude that God's plan was frustrated. Pharaoh's stubbornness is not an obstacle God failed to foresee; it is the stage on which He will make Himself known, verse 5.

The author also wants the readers to see where true authority lies. Two old men with a shepherd's staff stand before the throne of Egypt, surrounded by the court's experts. The staff and the serpent speak the language of Egyptian power, and God beats Egypt at its own symbols. Israel, who would face many rival powers and religions in Canaan and beyond, was meant to learn that imitation is not equality. Egypt's experts could copy a sign, but they could not win.

There is also a lesson in obedience. Twice the narrator notes that Moses and Aaron did 'just as the LORD had commanded,' verses 6 and 10. After two chapters of objection, Moses now simply obeys. The readers were meant to see that God's servants do not need to be impressive, only faithful to His word.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a unique moment. God appoints Moses 'like God to Pharaoh' and gives him a particular sign for a particular court. It does not teach that believers should seek to perform signs to prove the truth of God, nor that miraculous contests are the normal way God confronts unbelief. Jesus refused to perform signs on demand for those who asked in unbelief, Matthew 12:39.

Nor does it describe the ordinary way God deals with every sinner. Pharaoh's hardening is tied to his role in the history of redemption, as Romans 9:17 makes clear.

What does carry forward is the warning and the comfort. The warning is that repeated refusal of God's word hardens the heart, as 1 Samuel 6:6 and Hebrews 3:13 apply the story. The comfort is that no counterfeit power can finally stand against God. Scripture warns that false signs and wonders will continue, Matthew 24:24 and 2 Thessalonians 2:9, and that signs alone do not prove a message true, Deuteronomy 13:1-3. The test is always faithfulness to the word of the LORD.

debates.question: How can God harden Pharaoh's heart and still hold him responsible for his sin?

views.label: God's hardening is a judicial response to Pharaoh's own will
views.case: Pharaoh has already refused to know the LORD, Exodus 5:2, and in the early plagues his heart is either 'hardened' with no agent named, Exodus 7:13 and 7:22, or Pharaoh hardens it himself, Exodus 8:15 and 8:32. Only at Exodus 9:12 does the narrator first say 'the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart.' On this reading God confirms Pharaoh in the direction he chose, much as Romans 1:24 says God 'gave them over' to their desires.

views.label: God's hardening is sovereign and prior
views.case: God announces the hardening before Pharaoh makes any choice, Exodus 4:21 and 7:3, and Paul uses the story to say that God 'hardens whom He wants to harden,' Romans 9:18. He then anticipates the objection, 'Then why does God still find fault?' and answers with the potter's rights over the clay, Romans 9:19-20. This reading stresses that God's purpose governs the whole story.

views.label: Both are true at once without contradiction
views.case: Many Reformed and other interpreters hold that the text asserts God's sovereign hardening and Pharaoh's real, willing guilt together, as Proverbs 21:1 says the king's heart is in the LORD's hand while kings remain accountable. The narrator alternates the two descriptions deliberately.

debates.bearing: The text never lets Pharaoh plead that God made him do it; he 'sinned again and hardened his heart,' Exodus 9:34. And it never lets the reader think Pharaoh was outside God's control. The alternation is the teaching.

debates.question: How did Pharaoh's magicians reproduce the sign?

views.label: Skill and deception
views.case: Some think of trained snake handlers who could make a cobra rigid and then release it, or of sleight of hand. The phrase 'their magic arts,' verse 11, may suggest secret or hidden practice, and the magicians' later failure, Exodus 8:18, shows the limits of technique.

views.label: Real spiritual power opposed to God
views.case: Others take the text to describe genuine occult power. Scripture elsewhere speaks of real 'power, sign, and false wonder' worked by Satan, 2 Thessalonians 2:9, and of false prophets whose signs actually come to pass, Deuteronomy 13:2. Paul treats Jannes and Jambres as spiritual opponents of the truth, 2 Timothy 3:8.

debates.bearing: Exodus does not settle the mechanism because it is not the point. Whether by skill or by darker power, the magicians' serpents are swallowed. God's people need not fear counterfeit wonders, but they must not be persuaded by them either.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says literally, 'I have made you God to Pharaoh.' The word is elohim, and the BSB rightly adds 'like,' since Moses is not deified. He will stand before Pharaoh as God's representative, speaking with God's authority, and Aaron will be his navi, 'prophet.' The same arrangement was first described in Exodus 4:16, 'it will be as if you were God to him.' The verse gives one of the clearest definitions of a prophet in Scripture: one who speaks for another. Deuteronomy 18:18 makes the same point about the coming prophet, 'I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him,' echoing verse 2 here.

The hardening vocabulary is richer than English shows. In verse 3 God says, 'I will harden,' using qashah, a verb meaning to make hard, stiff or difficult, the root behind the 'stiff necked' people of Exodus 32:9. In verse 13, 'Pharaoh's heart was hardened,' the verb is chazaq, to be strong or firm, and it is intransitive: the heart grew strong, with no agent named. The BSB footnote offers 'stiffened or strengthened.' In the next verse, 7:14, a third term appears, kabed, 'heavy,' as the next footnote notes. Qashah, chazaq and kabed run through the plague cycle, and kabed makes a pointed play later, when God says He will 'gain honor,' literally make Himself heavy or glorious, through Pharaoh, Exodus 14:4 and 14:17-18. The heaviness of Pharaoh's heart becomes the weight of God's glory.

'Signs and wonders,' otot and mophetim, verse 3, is a paired phrase for miracles that point beyond themselves. An ot is a sign that signifies; a mophet is a portent that startles. Pharaoh's demand in verse 9, 'Perform a miracle,' uses mophet. Deuteronomy 6:22 and 26:8 remember the exodus in exactly these words, and Acts 2:22 describes Jesus as certified by God 'by miracles, wonders, and signs.'

'Divisions,' verse 4, is tsaba'ot, the word for hosts or armies, the same word as in the title 'LORD of Hosts.' Israel is not described as a mob of escaping slaves but as the LORD's ordered army, which is how they march out in Exodus 12:41.

The tannin of verses 9 to 12 is a larger or more monstrous creature than the nachash of Exodus 4:3. It is the word for the 'great sea creatures' of Genesis 1:21 and the 'dragon' of Isaiah 51:9 and 27:1.

Finally, 'swallowed up' in verse 12 is bala. The same verb returns at the climax of the exodus: 'You stretched out Your right hand, and the earth swallowed them up,' Exodus 15:12. What Aaron's staff does to the magicians' staffs, God's hand will do to Pharaoh's army. Isaiah uses the same verb for the final victory, 'He will swallow up death forever,' Isaiah 25:8, which Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:54.

typology.type: The serpent that swallows the serpents, Exodus 7:12
typology.fulfillment: The first sign in Pharaoh's court shows the whole contest in miniature: Egypt's powers are real enough to imitate, but they are consumed. The same verb, bala, describes the sea swallowing Egypt's army, Exodus 15:12, and Isaiah's promise that God 'will swallow up death forever,' Isaiah 25:8. Paul applies that promise to Christ's resurrection victory, 'Death has been swallowed up in victory,' 1 Corinthians 15:54. At the cross Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities,' Colossians 2:15. The type falls short in scale: Aaron's staff swallowed a few staffs, while Christ swallows up death itself.

typology.type: Moses 'like God,' with Aaron as his prophet, Exodus 7:1-2
typology.fulfillment: Moses stands before Pharaoh with God's authority but needs another to speak for him. In Christ the two roles are united and surpassed. He is not like God but is God, 'the one and only Son, who is Himself God,' John 1:18, and He is also the prophet who speaks only what He hears: 'I speak exactly what the Father has told Me to say,' John 12:50. God who once spoke through prophets 'has spoken to us by His Son,' Hebrews 1:1-2. The type breaks down at the point of weakness; Christ needs no spokesman and never falters.

typology.type: The magicians who resist Moses, Jannes and Jambres, 2 Timothy 3:8
typology.fulfillment: Paul reads the magicians as a pattern of every teacher who opposes the truth with an imitation of it. Their resistance was real but limited, and 'their folly will be plain to everyone,' 2 Timothy 3:9. The same pattern shows in Simon the sorcerer, astonished by 'the great signs and miracles' of the gospel, Acts 8:13, and in Elymas, who opposed Paul and was struck blind, Acts 13:8-11. The final form of it is the false prophet whose signs deceive, Revelation 13:13, who will be thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through the way God speaks. Exodus 7:1-2 gives a chain of revelation: God to Moses, Moses to Aaron, Aaron to Pharaoh. God's word reaches the world through mediators, and each link is weaker than the one before. Moses cannot speak well; Aaron can speak but has no authority of his own. Christ closes the gap. He is the Word who was with God and was God, John 1:1, and He says, 'I have not spoken on My own, but the Father who sent Me has commanded Me what to say,' John 12:49. Hebrews begins by saying that God, who spoke 'through the prophets,' has now spoken 'by His Son,' Hebrews 1:1-2.

It leads to Christ through the signs. Exodus 7:3 promises 'signs and wonders,' and Peter describes Jesus in the same words, 'a man certified by God to you by miracles, wonders, and signs,' Acts 2:22. As in Pharaoh's court, the signs Jesus performed did not by themselves produce faith. John records that 'although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him,' John 12:37, and then quotes Isaiah's words about blinded eyes and hardened hearts, John 12:40. The hardening of Exodus 7 finds a sobering echo in the response to the Son.

It leads to Christ through the contest with the serpent. The tannin that swallows the court's tanninim points, through the canonical thread of the dragon, to the one who crushes the ancient serpent's head, Genesis 3:15. When Jesus cast out demons, He said He did so 'by the finger of God,' Luke 11:20, the very phrase Pharaoh's defeated magicians would use in Exodus 8:19. The kingdom of God had come, and the strong man was being bound so that his house could be plundered, Matthew 12:29. At the cross He 'disarmed the powers and authorities,' Colossians 2:15, and by His death He destroyed 'him who holds the power of death,' Hebrews 2:14.

It leads to Christ through the swallowing. The verb that describes Aaron's staff consuming the others becomes, in Isaiah 25:8, the promise that God 'will swallow up death forever.' Paul sees that promise fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus and the future resurrection of His people, 1 Corinthians 15:54.

A caution is needed. Aaron's staff is not a symbol of the cross, and the serpent here is not the bronze serpent of John 3:14. The link to Christ runs through the canonical themes the passage opens, the word spoken by a mediator, signs met by hard hearts, and God's victory over every rival power, not through allegory of the staff.
study.god:
God's sovereignty in this passage extends to the ruler of the most powerful nation of the day. Before Pharaoh says a word, God tells Moses exactly how he will respond, verses 3 and 4, and the closing line confirms it, 'just as the LORD had said,' verse 13. The God of Israel is not reacting to Pharaoh; He is directing a story whose end He has already announced. Proverbs 21:1 says the king's heart is 'a waterway in the hand of the LORD,' and this chapter shows it.

That sovereignty is not arbitrary. God's goal is stated plainly: 'the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD,' verse 5. The plagues are revelation as well as judgment. Pharaoh had asked, 'Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?' Exodus 5:2, and God intends to answer the question, not only for Israel but for Egypt. Later He tells Pharaoh that the purpose reaches further still, 'that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth,' Exodus 9:16.

The passage also shows God as the God of order and of means. He could have freed Israel in a moment, but He works through a human spokesman, a staff, a sign, and a process of warning. He gives Pharaoh evidence before He gives him judgment. The first sign is harmless; no one is hurt when the serpents are swallowed. The patience of God comes before the plagues.

It shows God's supremacy over all other powers. The contest is not merely between Moses and the magicians but between the LORD and the gods of Egypt, as Exodus 12:12 and Numbers 33:4 later say. God does not deny that other powers exist; He shows that none can stand before Him. The magicians' serpents are real enough to imitate, and they are swallowed anyway.

Finally, the passage holds together God's sovereignty and human responsibility without apology. The same chapter that says 'I will harden' says that Pharaoh 'would not listen,' verse 13. Scripture does not dissolve the tension, and neither should we.

For worship, the passage calls for trust and humility. Believers can rest in a God whose purposes are not thwarted by powerful unbelief, and they must take seriously the warning that a heart which repeatedly refuses God's word can become hard. The right response to His signs is not to demand more of them but to listen.

crossReferences.note: The staff first became a snake at the burning bush, as a sign for Israel's belief. The BSB footnote notes that the creature there was a nachash, while here it is a tannin. The sign meant to persuade the elders now becomes a sign to confront Pharaoh.

God first set up the relationship between Moses and Aaron at the bush: Aaron would speak for Moses, 'and it will be as if you were God to him.' Exodus 7:1 extends the same arrangement to Pharaoh, answering Moses' repeated objection about his speech.

'You stretched out Your right hand, and the earth swallowed them up.' The Song of the Sea uses the same verb, bala, that describes Aaron's staff swallowing the magicians' staffs. The small sign in the court anticipates the final judgment on Pharaoh's army.

The psalmist recalls the exodus as the time God 'divided the sea' and 'smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea,' using the plural of tannin. The serpent sign of Exodus 7 belongs to this larger picture of God overpowering chaos and the powers opposed to Him.

Ezekiel calls Pharaoh the 'great monster who lies among his rivers,' the one who says, 'The Nile is mine.' The prophet makes explicit what Exodus 7 implies: the serpents of Pharaoh's court stand for Pharaoh himself, a monstrous power that God will overthrow.

The Philistine priests warn their people: 'Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?' Even Israel's enemies learned the lesson of the plague story. Pharaoh's hardening becomes a proverb for the folly of resisting God.

Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh from Exodus 9:16, 'I raised you up for this very purpose,' and concludes that God 'hardens whom He wants to harden.' He uses the story announced in Exodus 7:3 to defend God's freedom in mercy and judgment.

Paul names the magicians Jannes and Jambres and compares false teachers to them. Like the court magicians, such opponents can imitate godliness for a time, but 'they will not advance much further,' and their folly will be exposed.

Moses warns that a prophet whose sign or wonder actually comes to pass must still be rejected if he leads people after other gods. The magicians of Exodus 7:11 show why: signs can be imitated, so God's people must test every wonder by His word.

Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8, 'Death has been swallowed up in victory.' The verb of Exodus 7:12 becomes the language of resurrection. The last enemy is swallowed as surely as the magicians' serpents were, and the victory belongs to Christ.

study.oneStory:
Since the garden, the serpent has stood in Scripture for the power that sets itself against God and deceives humanity, Genesis 3:1. In Egypt that opposition takes the form of a king who has enslaved God's people and who wears a serpent on his crown. When Aaron's tannin swallows the court's serpents, the ancient conflict of Genesis 3:15 surfaces in a new setting. The seed of the woman, in the form of an enslaved people and their aged leaders, stands against the powers of the world, and God wins the first exchange before a single plague falls.

The passage also answers a question raised in the chapters just before it. Moses has protested twice that he is not fit to speak, Exodus 6:12 and 6:30. God's answer is that the power of the mission does not rest on Moses' eloquence. He appoints Aaron, gives a sign, and announces the end from the beginning. That pattern, weak messengers carrying God's word into a hostile world, will run through the whole story of Scripture, from the prophets to the apostles, who say, 'we have this treasure in jars of clay,' 2 Corinthians 4:7.

Looking forward, the scene introduces the long contest of the plagues and the hardening that leads to the sea. It is also the first of many confrontations between God's servants and the wisdom of the world's courts: Joseph before an earlier Pharaoh, Daniel in Babylon, Elijah before the prophets of Baal, 1 Kings 18:38-39, and Paul before Elymas the sorcerer, Acts 13:8-11.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who meets the great dragon not by imitation but by death and resurrection, and who swallows up death itself, 1 Corinthians 15:54. It reaches its end when 'the great dragon... that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan' is cast down, Revelation 12:9, and the devil who deceived the nations is thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10. In the new creation 'the sea was no more,' Revelation 21:1, the old home of the dragon gone, and God's people know, as Egypt was told they would, that He is the LORD.

quiz.q: What did God tell Moses about Pharaoh's heart before the plagues began?

options.text: That Pharaoh's heart was already soft toward Israel.
options.note: The text describes a hardened, resistant heart, not a soft or receptive one.

options.text: That Pharaoh would immediately obey after the first sign.
options.note: God explicitly says the opposite, that Pharaoh will not listen despite the signs.

options.text: Nothing was said about Pharaoh's heart at this point.
options.note: God speaks directly and specifically about hardening Pharaoh's heart in verses 3 to 4.

options.text: That He would harden Pharaoh's heart so that he would not listen even after many signs and wonders.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 state this plainly, before any plague or magician's contest occurs.

quiz.q: What sign did Aaron perform before Pharaoh?

options.text: He turned the Nile to blood.
options.note: That sign comes in the next chapter, not this one; here the sign is the staff becoming a serpent.

options.text: He threw down his staff and it became a serpent.
options.note: Verse 10 records this exact sign, performed as the LORD had commanded.

options.text: He performed no sign at all.
options.note: A specific sign, the staff becoming a serpent, is recorded clearly.

options.text: He called down hail from the sky.
options.note: The hail plague comes much later in the narrative, not in this scene.

quiz.q: How did Pharaoh's magicians respond to Aaron's sign?

options.text: They destroyed Aaron's staff.
options.note: The opposite happened; Aaron's staff swallowed theirs, not the reverse.

options.text: They immediately converted to worship the LORD.
options.note: The text shows continued hardness, not conversion, following this sign.

options.text: They were unable to perform any similar sign.
options.note: The text says they did the same thing by their magic arts, showing some ability to imitate, though it was overmatched.

options.text: They copied it by their magic arts, but Aaron's staff swallowed up theirs.
options.note: Verses 11 to 12 record both the magicians' imitation and its ultimate defeat.

quiz.q: What ages does the text give for Moses and Aaron at this confrontation?

options.text: Both were still young men in their twenties.
options.note: The text gives much older ages, eighty and eighty-three, not young adulthood.

options.text: Their ages are not recorded anywhere in Exodus.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly records both of their ages.

options.text: Moses was older than one hundred.
options.note: The specific age given for Moses is eighty, not over one hundred.

options.text: Moses was eighty and Aaron was eighty-three.
options.note: Verse 7 gives these specific ages, grounding the account in concrete historical detail.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament refer back to the Egyptian magicians in this passage?

options.text: The New Testament never mentions this episode again.
options.note: Paul directly references these magicians by name in 2 Timothy 3:8.

options.text: The magicians are said to have become apostles.
options.note: There is no biblical basis for this claim; they remain a negative example throughout.

options.text: Paul names them Jannes and Jambres as a type of those who oppose the truth and are eventually exposed.
options.note: 2 Timothy 3:8-9 names these magicians directly and applies their pattern to end-times opposition to the truth.

options.text: Jesus commends the magicians for their skill.
options.note: No such commendation exists; Paul uses them as a negative example of opposing the truth.

questions: God declared in advance that He would harden Pharaoh's heart, holding sovereignty and human responsibility together without fully explaining the mystery. How do you hold on to trust in God's sovereignty even in situations you cannot fully understand?

Egypt's magicians could copy the first sign, but not withstand Aaron's staff swallowing theirs. Where in your life are you relying on a counterfeit power or solution that cannot ultimately stand against God's greater power?
Pharaoh witnessed a genuine miracle and still hardened his heart. What warning does this give you about the danger of seeing God's work clearly and still refusing to respond rightly to Him?
Moses and Aaron were eighty and eighty-three years old when this mission truly began. How does their example encourage you if you feel you have missed your window for God to use you significantly?

God patiently multiplied signs before Pharaoh even though He knew the outcome in advance. Where do you need to trust God's patience with someone who keeps resisting Him, rather than giving up on them?

translationNotes.note: The word for serpent here, tannin, is a stronger term than nachash used for Moses' sign in Exodus 4:3, suggesting a larger or more monstrous creature, fitting for a formal royal sign before Pharaoh's whole court.

The magicians' ability to replicate the sign by their magic arts has been understood variously as demonic power, skilled illusion, or both; the text does not specify the mechanism, only that it was ultimately overmatched.
